Contract & Project Hiring in the UAE: Why Flexible Roles Could Be Your Smartest Career Move in 2024

Flexible Hiring Is Booming Across the UAE — And That's Good News for You If you've been scanning UAE job listings lately, you've probably noticed something: a growing number of roles are tagged as "contract," "project-based," or "fixed-term." This isn't a coincidence. Recruiter commentary and live outsourcing vacancies across the Emirates point to a clear trend — employers are leaning hard into flexible staffing to stay agile. The momentum behind this shift is strong, and it's reshaping how work gets done from Dubai to Abu Dhabi. Sectors leading the charge include construction, technology, healthcare, IT, energy, and facilities management. Think about it: with mega-projects tied to Dubai's 2040 Urban Master Plan, Abu Dhabi's energy transition, and the UAE's relentless push into AI and digital infrastructure, companies need specialist talent fast — but not always permanently. Contract and project hiring lets them scale teams up for a specific build, rollout, or go-live, then adjust as priorities change.

We’re hiring: 
Sales Associate. Remote, India-based, full-time contract.
The students who message us are carrying a lot: an education loan, a family counting on them, and a job search that hasn’t worked yet. Many have been burned by services that promised too much. They don’t need a pushy salesperson. They need someone who listens, tells them the truth, and helps them pick the right plan.
At Jaithraya, we help international students find the right job, the right résumé, and we apply for them. As our Sales Associate, you’re the first real person they talk to.
What you’ll do:
→ Reply to students who reach out on Instagram and WhatsApp. Inbound only, no cold calling
→ Understand each student’s situation before suggesting anything
→ Guide them to the plan that fits, and help them get started
→ Check in with your customers in their first weeks so they get real value
→ Ask happy customers to refer their friends
→ Keep every conversation logged in our lead tracker
Our rules, and the reason students trust us:
→ Never promise a job, an interview or a visa outcome
→ Never give visa or immigration advice. Those questions go to the student’s DSO (their school’s international student office) or an immigration attorney
→ Never handle a customer’s card, bank details or passwords
→ Never invent a testimonial, a number or a result
→ No mass messaging, ever
You’re a fit if you:
→ Listen first, then guide. You never push
→ Speak and write clear English (Telugu or Hindi is a plus)
→ Know WhatsApp, Instagram, AI chat tools (like ChatGPT or Claude) and online tools
→ Stay calm and honest when someone says “is this a scam?” or “it’s too expensive”
→ Care whether the customer is still happy three months later, not just whether they paid
Good to have: experience in sales, counselling, customer success or study-abroad services.
The details:
* Work from home: you need your own laptop, stable internet and headphones
* Pay discussed after the interview
* You work directly with the founder
How to apply: email HR at bhavishya@jaithraya.com or the founder at anwarrashidshaik@jaithraya.com with the subject “Sales – where you saw this post” (e.g. “Sales – LinkedIn”) and include:
Your CV
A few lines on why this role suits you
One time you helped someone make a decision without pushing them
Selection: application review → short intro call → a role-play (a typical student question, handled live) → final interview.

2x revenue, flat hiring: your competitor's new plan.

According to Bloomberg, Applied Materials expects to double revenue over the next few years without a matching rise in hiring. The lever is AI tools in product development and quality control.

That one sentence is the whole story. Growth used to be priced in headcount. Every new contract meant another hire, another salary, another layer of coordination.

For a small business, the math is even harsher. If revenue is capped by how many hours your team spends copying data between systems, every sale you add makes the business heavier, not stronger.

The companies that automate the repetitive layer first don't just save money. They get to say yes to demand their competitors have to turn away.

So before posting the next job opening, list what that role actually does all day. Some of it needs judgment. A lot of it is a workflow waiting to be built.

If your SEO guru's strategy is to create 100 pages targeting 100 keywords, you might be paying for a long-term problem instead of a solution.

Google's September 2026 spam update offers a serious warning.

An analysis of 33,643 websites found that 10% lost at least half their Google search traffic during one week of the rollout, compared with a 2% baseline.

Among the reported losing patterns were pages created from the same template, with only the location or keyword changed.

One page for Mombasa.
One for Diani.
One for Watamu.
One for Kilifi.

Same content. Different location names.
More pages. More keywords. But not necessarily more value.

And this is exactly why, before hiring an SEO expert, you should ask to see their SEO/GEO strategy.

Don't just ask how many keywords they will rank you for.
Ask:
→ How will this strategy make my business more useful to potential customers?
→ How will each page provide unique, relevant information?
→ How will you build my authority beyond my own website?
→ How will this help my business become discoverable in both Google search and AI-generated recommendations?
→ How will we measure meaningful results beyond keyword positions?

If the entire strategy revolves around publishing more pages, targeting more keyword variations, and chasing rankings, without explaining how those pages will serve real customer needs, that's a red flag.

Multiple service and location pages can be valuable. 
But each needs a genuine purpose.
Show real projects. Share original photos. 
Explain your services clearly. Demonstrate local expertise. 
Answer questions your customers actually ask.

Give people—and search engines—something worth discovering.

At Prolific VA, we believe SEO and GEO should be built around useful content, clear business information, and genuine authority, not just page volume.

Before you sign that contract, ask your SEO guru to walk you through the strategy.

If the keywords disappeared from the plan, would there still be a compelling reason for those pages to exist?
That question could save you months of wasted effort.

While the world was distracted by daily AI breakthroughs from Worldbank IMF meeting in Bangkok, a silent war for human capital fundamentally redrew the map of global innovation.

The catalyst was a $100,000 surcharge on US H-1B visas in late 2025, which priced out mid-tier tech hiring overnight and unleashed a wave of borderless talent. Competitors didnt blink. 

Nations like China, South Korea, and the UK immediately slashed friction, rolling out sponsor-free, fast-track visas to capture the spillover. 

But what did Indonesia do while we were sleeping?We accidentally engineered a Consumer Trap. Indonesia requires 12 million digital talents by 2030, yet we face a staggering deficit of 9 million. 

Paradoxically, thousands of world-class engineers, AI specialists, and tech founders already reside in hubs like Bali, Canggu and Ubud—but they remain economically invisible. Our current policy treats mobile talent merely as high-spending tourists. The Remote Worker Visa (E33G) explicitly bars digital nomads from contracting with local firms. 

We successfully import their foreign income into our cafes and villas, but we legally forbid them from integrating with our domestic ecosystem. The result? Zero Transfer of Technology (ToT) and zero Transfer of Knowledge (ToK). 

To wake up and convert this foreign presence into national capability, we must pivot from passive residence to active absorption: Unlock Productive Rights: Amend the E33G to allow digital nomads to legally contract with, consult for, and mentor Indonesian startups, converting them from untracked consumers into active economic contributors. 

Create Rules-Based Tracks: Replace subjective, capital-focused permits with transparent, points-based digital talent routes that professionals can verify in advance. Embrace Diaspora Linkages: 

Shift from punitive retention by obligation (like rigid scholarship return bonds) to validating remote R&D and advising contributions, fostering true brain circulation. Talent is now a contested, highly mobile factor of production. 

It is time to wake up. We must give global minds the structural runway to build with us, not just live near us. How should emerging markets balance local labor protection with the urgent need for global tech transfer?

Week 3 - Building a Privacy Career in Public

10/12/2026

I’m looking for my first dedicated remote privacy role, and I figured I might as well build the career in public. 🙏

Well, things escalated. 😂

Last week I was excited because one privacy person responded to me:

This week, people started introducing me to other people.

I had reached out to Daniel Barber with some questions about breaking into privacy. Wednesday morning, Daniel asked me:

“Are you a member of Privacy Roundtable?”

I was not.

He explained that it’s a large invite-only Slack community for privacy professionals and thought the people there could help answer my questions.

Then he invited me.

So naturally, I immediately started asking questions. 😂

I asked people who hire privacy talent, manage privacy teams, or recently broke into the field how they had seen that first dedicated privacy role happen.

Hannah Poteat gave me a distinction that changed how I’m thinking about my search: 0-to-1 versus 1-to-N.

A company hiring its first privacy person often needs someone senior who can build the function.

But once that person gets headcount, they start hiring analysts, privacy ops, governance, and program roles underneath them.

So maybe I shouldn’t only ask:

“Which companies need privacy?”

I should ask:

“Which privacy teams are starting to grow?”

I asked Hannah how you find those companies.

Her answer was interesting: sometimes you don’t.

Some jobs never get posted publicly. People share them inside communities like Privacy Roundtable and local IAPP networks.

Suddenly this whole “talk to privacy people” experiment made considerably more sense. 😂

Then Teaghan told me about his own path.

Only a year ago, privacy was around 30% of his job. He sent around a dozen applications, found the right opening, and landed a full-time privacy role.

I asked whether having privacy as only part of his old job hurt him.

He said no.

Working on a small team actually gave him broad ownership. His advice was to own as much as possible, DSARs, risk assessments, notices, processes, and show employers you can work independently.

That sounded VERY familiar.

My small-business consulting work has given me room to work across DSAR processes, retention, vendor privacy, DPIAs, policies, and process design.

I’ve wondered whether that experience would look too small.

Maybe the breadth is actually part of the value.

Ben Archer added another piece: early privacy hires can become “privacy unicorns” responsible for everything from regulations and contracts to DPIAs, risk, and AI governance. As teams mature, they start hiring analysts for more focused work.

I also asked whether CIPP/US would materially change my chances.

Vandana’s advice:

Lead with the experience.

Meanwhile, Michael Ariyo pointed me toward the career-support community and an upcoming discussion with Dr. Kyle David about breaking into privacy.

Let go by my long-term employer in December, I spent 8 months looking for work. 

To be fair, I gave myself a pass for the first 5 months but I was still looking and occasionally applying. 

The main thing I did was to reconnect with people I'd worked with but hadn't seen for some time. 

If you've been out of work and looking for a while, I hope these tips help you out or at the very least reminds you that it *is* challenging and that you're not alone.

* It's good to practice retirement if you get the chance.

* Networking is not a dirty word
Other people wish they caught up with ex-colleagues more often too.
Connecting for connecting's sake is the way to go. It doesn't have to be about a role or an introduction, just staying connected. 

* When you have work, keep 'sharpening the saw' with skills you may not need now but will be useful in the future - PM, AI, finances, contract mgmt, govt process

* Just because a chat, or even an interview goes well, it doesn't mean you've got the job. There are factors outside of your control - approvals, contracts and other dependencies. Don't take it personally but focus on what *is* in your control. 

* Stay on top of industry news, you never know when it might be useful.

* Applying for jobs through Seek is basically useless unless you have a contact at the target firm that can refer you. 
Yes, even if you get hold of the contact officer (if you can).
 
* Some jobs take months to land - negotiations, approvals, onboarding and more. 

* Apparently just being qualified and experienced is not enough, your CV also needs to be attractively optimised *and* you need to be lucky. 

* Scrolling LinkedIn is not job hunting. 
In fact, it can be depressing and demotivating because so many posts are about problems with hiring - industry downturns, AI resume filters, recruiter ghosting and more awful. 

* If you're not having any luck in your familiar industry vertical, consider stretching to other industries and/or areas. 
It seems counter-intuitive because if you can't get hired where you have experience, why would you get hired where you don't? Different industries go through different phases - economically, technically and expand/contract. You may find that your skills are translatable.

Good luck out there!

- Two-thirds of top-performing companies now have tech leaders deep in enterprise strategy.

I've seen this movie before. We cut the pipeline to save money today, and in a few years, we're overpaying to poach mid-level talent because nobody trained them. That "efficiency" starts looking expensive.

- Hiring, upskilling, and vendor strategy are the same lever now. Pull one, the others shift.

- Fewer, more senior hires can work—but only if you invest in keeping their judgment sharp as headcount shrinks.

- Vendor contracts built for a labor-heavy world reward activity over outcomes. That gets expensive fast when AI makes development leaner.

- Cutting grad pipelines to fund AI might be the most consequential decision on this list, and it's the one getting the least boardroom scrutiny.

The question I keep asking APAC execs: If we don't hire the juniors now, who runs the show in 2031?

Your biggest risk isn't AI readiness, it's the talent shortage you're manufacturing today that'll resurface as a costly mid-career crisis.

Fix the pipeline. Now.

REST, GraphQL, SOAP… choosing an API isn't just about knowing the names. Its about understanding what your system actually needs. 👇

Think about the applications you use every day:
🌦️ A weather app fetching live data
🔐 A website handling login requests
🏦 A banking platform processing transactions
📊 A dashboard retrieving data from multiple services
🤝 Two companies connecting their systems

All of these can involve APIs, but the way they communicate can be very different.
Heres a quick breakdown of the types shown in this visual:
🔹 REST APIs - Common for web apps, product data, and authentication.
🔹 SOAP APIs - Often used in enterprise environments where strict contracts and established integration standards matter.
🔹 GraphQL APIs - Useful when clients need flexibility in choosing exactly which data they want.
🔹 Internal APIs - Connect services within an application or organization, such as a frontend, backend, and database layer.
🔹 Partner APIs - Enable integrations with external businesses, payment providers, booking platforms, and other services.
🔹 Data-Sharing APIs - Allow systems to exchange information across platforms, such as logistics, finance, or healthcare data.

One important thing to remember: these categories arent all mutually exclusive. REST, SOAP, and GraphQL describe API approaches, while internal, partner, and data-sharing APIs describe how or where APIs are used.

When designing a system, the better questions are:
→ Who will consume the API?
→ What data needs to be exchanged?
→ How should authentication and security work?
→ What performance, reliability, and compatibility requirements exist?

Understanding these trade-offs is what helps you move beyond simply using APIs to designing better backend systems.

I used Postman for 18 months. Thought I was doing API testing. Then a senior interviewer asked me one question. I had no answer.

"How do you validate that your API hasn't broken its contract with 3 downstream consumers?"

I said: "I'd check the response in Postman."

He nodded. Interview ended shortly after.

That failure taught me what API testing actually means at a senior level.

What juniors answer:

Send request → check status code → check response body

What seniors answer:

🔹 Contract validation across consumers
🔹 Schema drift detection
🔹 State injection to remove UI dependency
🔹 Mocking downstream failures to test resilience
🔹 Performance degradation thresholds, not just pass or fail

The difference isn't tools. It's the questions you know to ask before writing a single test.

Postman is where API exploration begins. Not where API testing ends.

It's the mindset shift most SDETs take years to make.

(Yes, the wonderful Iris Apfel! Still working in her 90s.) 

There’s a lot of talk on LinkedIn about the challenges many older workers face in finding jobs, particularly when AI’s front and centre of a lot of hiring decisions. 

I can’t reduce hirers’ reliance on AI or encourage every employer to take a smarter view, but I CAN help you write a CV that talks up the benefits of being an older worker. (And there are many!) 

My advice (from coaching many others in this situation – and being an ‘older’ worker myself): consider formatting your CV based on impact. 

Group your experience under headers that summarise what you’ve achieved in your career – with a nod to the competencies and keywords in the job ad. 

Projects delivered on time. Successful negotiations. New products developed. That sort of thing. 

Then list your achievements under these headers, across your work history. Chances are you’ll have several examples under each header. (Great! Your experience is solid. No one-trick ponies here!) 

Finally, list your roles chronologically (and briefly) at the end of your CV, covering the past 15 years. 

In my experience, an impact CV talks up what matters – your impact. It takes the focus off dates. Downplays those ‘filler’ roles and contracts that pepper many CVs these days (but pay the bills). And satisfies both ATS (AI) and in-person recruiters. 

Added bonus? You’re likely to feel chuffed about what you’re achieved. Give it a go! I'm here to help.

A cloud credit commitment is no longer commercial spend; it is equity in disguise
On 22 August, the UK Competition and Markets Authority issued updated guidance clarifying when foundation model partnerships trigger merger control scrutiny under the Enterprise Act. The guidance targets minority equity stakes, multi-year cloud compute arrangements, and talent acqui-hires. The market has spent two years drafting these transactions as commercial vendor agreements; the CMA has now classified them as structural acquisitions of material influence.
The standard structuring assumption was that avoiding voting control kept a transaction outside the merger regime. That works for industrial joint ventures; it fails for artificial intelligence. When a hyperscaler provides five hundred million dollars in compute credits alongside a ten per cent equity stub and exclusive distribution rights, the commercial dependency confers operational veto power without a single board seat. The CMA recognised what corporate counsel knew privately: in capital-intensive model training, access to compute is control.
The predictable defence is that intervention will choke venture funding for European and British frontier labs. That conflates transaction friction with prohibition. The guidance does not ban hyperscaler partnerships; it strips them of their procedural invisibility. A transaction that would previously close on a standard procurement contract and a SAFE note now requires substantive competition review, jurisdictional filings, and multi-month closing conditions.
For a GC or corporate development lead on Monday, this resets your term sheet playbook. If you are structuring an AI investment that pairs equity with infrastructure access, compute exclusivity, or key-person hiring, you must run a UK merger control assessment before signing. Build a CMA call-in condition into the long-stop date, and do not assume that calling an allocation a "commercial discount" removes it from the regulator's jurisdictional calculus.
The CMA did not create a new competition threshold. It looked past the commercial label and found the merger hidden beneath it.

#OpenToWork - the R in SRE.

Officially, the R stands for Reliability.  But in my work, it means Relentless.
Relentless about toil.  If I do a task once, I automate it.  That 2 am page I fix once becomes the health check that stops it from happening again.  The whole point is engineering the manual work out of the system.

Relentless about learning.  The stack never holds still - Kubernetes, the tooling, the failure modes all keep moving, so I move with them.  Even after decades, I treat every incident as a chance to get better, not just something to survive.

Relentless about uptime.  Self-healing defaults, SLOs that only page for real user impact, Kubernetes handling recovery a team would otherwise do by hand.  The cluster stays up without anyone babysitting it at 2 am.

I bring that same relentlessness to my job search.  I built an AI pipeline with Claude Code - curated daily boards, a dedup ledger so I never re-apply, and résumés and cover letters that always pass an adversarial agent review.  That approach works - I start a new contract next week.

The contract's a solid start, but I'm looking for a full-time home - a remote Staff or Principal SRE or Platform role with a team that wants infrastructure engineered to run itself.  If you're hiring or know someone who is, a comment, DM, or tag of the right person goes a long way.

Could AI recruitment be screening out the very experience organisations need?

I’m not usually one for posting, but as my current contract is coming to an end, it’s got me thinking.

I didn’t go to university. I was too busy working, learning and building my career.

Over 24 years, I’ve gained extensive experience in technology, enterprise transformation, SAP, governance and organisational change — largely through real-world delivery.

With AI increasingly being used in recruitment, I wonder how effectively these systems recognise experience that doesn’t fit traditional academic or career pathways.

I’m not questioning the value of qualifications. But having qualifications and being qualified to do the job aren’t always the same thing.

This comes back to something I strongly believe about AI implementation: we need to understand what we’re trying to achieve and ensure we’re not simply automating existing limitations and biases.

Are we identifying genuine capability, or just finding candidates who tick the right boxes?

And who is checking what AI might be missing?

I’d be interested to hear how others see this, particularly recruiters and hiring managers.

If you know me, you know I love nerding out over sports stats: box scores, shooting splits, the advanced metrics nobody asked for. So when our team put together a roundup of finance staffing data (link in the comments), I was intrigued. 

Two numbers jumped out.
87% of finance leaders report a critical accounting talent shortage.
63% plan to increase contract or interim hiring.

That second number is the one I keep coming back to. Bringing in interim help used to be the finance version of a panic trade. Your starter goes down, you scramble, and you hope it holds through the rest of the season.

The best front offices don’t operate that way. They build depth with purpose. They know who steps in when a key player goes down, and they keep specialists ready for specific situations. Finance leaders are starting to build their teams the same way, planning interim talent into system implementations, audit prep, growth pushes, and the gap between a controller’s resignation and the replacement’s first day.

A couple more insights from the report:
→ An understaffed team is a risk problem before it’s a workload problem. Late closes, control gaps, and one resignation away from a stall. Thin benches lose games.
→ AI isn’t reducing the need for experienced people. It’s a better playbook, but someone still has to run it and sign off on the numbers.

The finance team of the next decade will be a roster: full-time starters, outsourced processes, and interim experts brought in exactly when the work calls for them.

Finance leaders: how are you building your bench heading into year-end?

Here's a profit leak I'd look for in almost any service business: work your employees completed but nobody billed the customer for.
⠀
Take an illustrative company completing 4,000 service jobs a year.
⠀
Technicians sometimes perform additional work, replace parts or handle problems outside the original scope.
⠀
They record what happened in their service notes, but the office doesn't always catch the extra charges before sending the invoice.
⠀
Suppose 8% of jobs include $150 in additional work that was never billed.
⠀
That's $48,000 in potential missed annual revenue.
⠀
AI-assisted job review can compare technician notes, work orders, customer approvals and invoices. It flags possible missing charges before the invoice goes out.
⠀
A human still checks whether the work was authorized, whether the contract allows the charge and whether the customer actually owes the money.
⠀
If the company identifies and collects just 60% of those missed charges, that's another $28,800 in annual revenue.
⠀
Clearly illustrative. It's not automatically $28,800 in profit, although much of the work's cost may already have been incurred.
⠀
The real opportunity is collecting more of the revenue you've already earned without hiring another technician or buying another truck.
⠀
Before spending more money finding new customers, make sure you're billing correctly for the work you're already doing.
⠀
If your company is generating plenty of revenue but not enough profit, DM me "PROFIT."

Verification is the product when a model can ship a plausible wrong answer in seconds.

I have been in rooms where "we shipped the agent" meant a demo path worked twice. Spot checks looked fine. Then a hard case hit a customer and the team discovered nobody owned the eval suite, the grading rubric, or the human review path for the ugly edges. Trust broke at verification, where ownership was never assigned.

(Operator observation, plain label: I am not citing a lab result here. I am describing the hiring ask I keep hearing from teams that already launched.)

What changes when you treat verification as the product: QA and eval seats stop being an afterthought on the eng req. Someone owns what "green" means. Hard cases have a human path. Output grading is written down so juniors are not guessing. Contract language that only promises "best effort review" is often a confession that verification was never staffed.

Speed still matters. Ship-fast without a verification owner just moves the risk into CS and trust. The scarce hire is often the person who can build the harness and live in the failure modes (more than the person who only prompts well on stage).

If your next open req is "AI engineer" and the scorecard has no line for verification ownership, add one before you post it. The interview changes. The person you hire changes. The customer feels it either way.

What if an AI agent could do more than understand what happened inside an enterprise?
What if it could explore what could happen instead?
What if demand dropped 20%?
A major customer defaulted?
A supplier failed?
Interest rates increased?
Production capacity declined?
Hiring froze?
Costs suddenly increased?
This is the idea behind Xpert Systems’ Connected Enterprise What-If datasets.
A Connected Enterprise links customers, suppliers, employees, products, contracts, operations, transactions and financial records across time.
The What-If version goes further.
Introduce a scenario or shock—and let its consequences propagate through the enterprise.
Supplier disruption → Procurement → Inventory shortage → Production/Fulfillment → Customer impact → Revenue → Cash flow → Financial statements
One event can create second- and third-order consequences across the business.
Now an AI agent can reason beyond:
What happened?
It can investigate:
What happens if something changes?
Which processes are affected?
What are the downstream consequences?
What happens to revenue, costs, cash and operations?
What actions could management take?
Which decision produces a better outcome?
This creates powerful environments for AI model training, AI agent training, scenario analysis, counterfactual reasoning, evaluation and benchmarking.
Instead of testing whether an AI agent can retrieve information, we can test whether it can reason through an enterprise under changing conditions.
That is a much harder AI problem—and potentially a much more valuable one.
And we don't only build Connected Enterprises.
Xpert Systems also buys and licenses real-world enterprise data that can legally be used for AI training, evaluation, benchmarking and research.
We are interested in legally licensable historical and operational data including:
ERP • CRM • Accounting • Procurement • Manufacturing • Supply Chain • Engineering • HR • Transactions • Contracts • Documents • Emails
The goal is to move enterprise AI from simply understanding what happened toward reasoning about what could happen—and what to do next.
Building AI models or AI agents that need enterprise-scale What-If environments?
Or have real enterprise data you have the legal right to license for AI?

A React app usually isn’t slow because of React. 

It’s slow because one small state change re-renders half the page, and nobody notices until users start complaining. 

I ran into exactly this on a production app. I didn’t rewrite anything. I profiled it, found the components re-rendering for no reason, and fixed them with memoization and cleaner hooks. Unnecessary re-renders dropped by about 40%. 

Honestly, this is the part of the job I enjoy most: finding the real problem instead of guessing. 

I’m Sameer, a full stack developer based in Lahore with 2+ years of experience. Mostly React and Next.js on the frontend, with Node, Express and MongoDB on the backend. 

So far I’ve owned 20+ production components and integrated 15+ REST APIs using Redux Toolkit, RTK Query and TanStack Query. I’ve also worked on authentication, role-based access and a few AI features. 

I’m open to full-time, contract, freelance and remote roles.

HIRING!  Ontology Architect, Full-Time | Contract-to-Hire | Remote (U.S.) 
OtterSoft is building an AI-ready workforce management platform powered by a sophisticated semantic data architecture. We are hiring our first Ontology Architect to design and own the semantic model at the core of our platform: how people, credentials, organizations, facilities, units, shifts, assignments, and contracts relate, and the business rules that govern how they interact. 

Your ontology will provide the foundation for intelligent matching, compliance automation, demand forecasting, and AI-agent workflows used by our customers and internal teams. This is a foundational architecture role for someone who can transform complex business processes and disconnected data sources into a scalable, governed semantic model. You will define how data is structured, connected, interpreted, and used by applications and AI agents to support reliable decisions and automated workflows. 

You will work closely with product, engineering, data, and business stakeholders to establish the architecture, technical standards, and governance practices that support the platform as it grows.

Contact for more details or submit your resume: kathy.martinez@ottersoft.com.
